messages.subject: Model Definition Properties for Mongolian Wild Camel Study
parts:
We have conducted a population study of wild Bactrian camels in the Gobi Strictly Protected Area in south-western Mongolia. We have some questions regarding the Model Definition Properties and which settings are suitable to use for our particular study. Please find our questions and examples in the attached file.   


We eagerly await your response!

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Model Definition Properties for Mongolian Wild Camel Study
parts:
Nice to renew your acquaintance again Moojii.  Looks as though you are putting your distance sampling training to use.

Your analysis highlights a subtle point when performing stratified analyses; I am not surprised you were confused by what you saw.  It makes such a nice example, I would like to be able to use it in some of our training materials if you would permit. 

Here is my interpretation.  Post-stratification is assumed to take place over the same geographic area; you might remember the lecture notes from your 2011 training wherein we demonstrated post-stratification in association with two different species occupying the same study area.  We could use post-stratification to produce species-specific estimates and then we could add together the species-specific density estimates to produce a combined density estimate (this is how your second analysis was performed, look at the screenshot on page 5 of your document).

In contrast a 'regular' stratified analysis is thought to take place in geographically distinct portions of the study area.  Stratum-specific density estimates are produced by Distance, but then the question becomes how to combine those stratum-specific estimates?  There are several ways to define the combination in Distance.

It makes most sense to take the average of the stratum-specific densities as an estimate of the density in the entire study area (the densities of the two regions should not be added together).  But there are different ways to calculate an average.  Looking at page 3 of the document you attached, you asked Distance to produce an estimate for the entire study area as the mean of the stratum-specific estimates weighted by the area of the strata.  I believe this is not the proper weighting to apply because the size of the "Limited" stratum is quite large (>20000km^2) but you have very little sampling effort in that stratum.  I would consider using weighting by "effort" which you can select in Distance, as being a more appropriate weighting scheme.  Weighting by effort places more weight on the strata where there was more sampling effort and less weight in less-intensively studied regions.

In the final assessment, the conclusive analysis is based upon your judgement, specifically regarding the information you gathered from the outer (limited) zone.  I would be reluctant to make inference to 20000km^2 based upon 9 sampling points all of which are clustered in the northern portion of this region.  I would be inclined to remove the limited zone from your analysis (as you did in analysis 3) because of the limited information you have for that stratum.

You then need to decide whether the resulting overall density estimate should be the weighted average of the 2 (core and conservation) strata and whether the weighting should be by stratum size (the result you have for analysis 3) or weighted by sampling effort.  Given you have 32 points in each core and conservation, it is easy to calculate by hand that this alternative weighting produces an overall density estimate of 0.0192 per km^2 (compared to the 0.0204 per km^2 in analysis 3).  This mean density translates to an estimated camel abundance of 496 using the weighting by effort compared to 527 weighting by area.  The difference between those two values is small (6%) relative to the size of the respective coefficients of variation (~40%).

I hope that helps you with your analysis.  Good for you to have completed the survey and diagnosed a curiosity with your analysis.

On 11/12/2015 02:23, Moojii Myagmar wrote:
Dear Eric,

I'm so glad to hear from you. I was one of students from the Introduction course in 2011. May be you remember me as I was one and only Asian face that time :)

Thank you so much for your prompt reply. Let me try to answer these questions below.

1. the map legend suggests they are points:  did you conduct point transect surveys or line transect surveys?

    Yes, we did conduct point counts.

2. Were the survey locations selected at random?

    Yes, that were randomly selected. We've placed random points throughout the protected area first and removed the points which are inaccessible. Additionally, in the same time interval on the way back people were stopping for observations which may look like a pattern on the map.

3. Were the zones you describe an element of placing your points, or where the zones only considered after the points were determined (that speaks to the issue of whether to stratify or post-stratify)?  The answers to your questions should be reached without consulting the results.  It is bad practice to choose the analysis method as a result of the answer the method provides.

    The zones have been considered after we determined the points.
    We are confused with the analysis. We thought the post-stratification suits to our data, but after we read the program manual which says Stratum Data Layer recommended for a geographic stratification, we got confused then.

Thank you very much again, Eric!
Hope to hear from you soon.

Best wishes,
Moojii




On Thu, Dec 10, 2015 at 6:35 PM, Eric Rexstad <er...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:
Moojii

Thanks for sending your questions in such an organised manner.  It make day a few days for me to find time to address them (someone else may reply before I do).

May I ask you a couple of questions about your surveys: the map legend suggests they are points:  did you conduct point transect surveys or line transect surveys?  Were the survey locations selected at random?  Were the zones you describe an element of placing your points, or where the zones only considered after the points were determined (that speaks to the issue of whether to stratify or post-stratify)?  The answers to your questions should be reached without consulting the results.  It is bad practice to choose the analysis method as a result of the answer the method provides.
